source_text: Corpus nostrum cum movetur, aut extrinsecus, aut intrinsecus movetur. Non moveri illud extrinsecus, ex eo patet: quod neque impulsione, neque tractione movetur, sicut ea quae sunt inanimata. Cum autem moveatur intrinsecus, non tamen naturaliter movetur ut ignis. Nam ignis quandiu est, nunquam motum intermittit: at corpus ubi mortuum fuerit, moveri desinit, licet tamen sit corpus. Quare si neque extrinsecus movetur, sicut inanimata; neque naturaliter, velut ignis: manifestum est moveri ab Anima, quae etiam vitam ipsi subministrat. Si igitur corpori nostro vitam ab anima praeberi constet, anima etiam ex suis effectis cognoscitur.
thought_title: The body moves by the soul, not by outside force or natural tendency
orientation: Gregory argues that the living body moves intrinsically by the soul, since it is moved neither from outside like inanimate objects nor by an unceasing natural tendency like fire; therefore the soul is known from its effect of giving life and motion to the body.
pass_a_gloss: Our body, when it is moved, is moved either from outside or from inside. That it is not moved from outside is clear from this: that it is moved neither by pushing nor by pulling, as those things that are inanimate. But when it is moved from inside, nevertheless it is not moved naturally as fire. For fire, as long as it exists, never ceases its motion: but the body, when it has become dead, ceases to be moved, although it is still a body. Therefore if it is moved neither from outside, like inanimate things; nor naturally, like fire: it is clear that it is moved by the Soul, which also supplies life to it. If therefore it is established that life is supplied to our body by the soul, the soul also is known from its effects.

choices.english: neither by pushing nor by pulling
choices.why: Literal rendering of the two ablative nouns denoting the modes of external motion applied to inanimate objects; avoids the single word 'impulsion' which would obscure the paired contrast.
rejected: neither by impulse nor by traction

choices.why: Preserves the spatial adverb 'intrinsecus' as a source of motion, matching the earlier 'extrinsecus'; 'internally' would be acceptable but less precise for the adverbial force.
Keeps the comparative 'ut' with the noun 'fire' to show the likeness of motion; 'like fire' would be looser.
rejected: moves by nature as fire does

choices.why: Literal: 'intermittit' with 'motum' (accusative) = ceases/interrupts its motion; 'stops moving' would lose the noun.

choices.english: although it is still a body
choices.why: 'Licet' + indicative = concessive 'although'; 'tamen' reinforces the concession; 'though it is a body' drops 'still'.
rejected: even though it remains a body

choices.english: it is established that life is supplied ... by the soul
choices.why: 'Constet' impersonal passive = 'it is established/agreed'; 'praeberi' passive infinitive = 'to be supplied'; 'ab anima' agent. 'Supplied' captures the benefactive sense of 'praebere'.
rejected: it is clear that life is given by the soul
it stands firm that life is provided by the soul

pass_b_english: Our body moves either from outside or from inside. It is clear that it is not moved from outside, because it is moved neither by pushing nor by pulling, the way inanimate things are. Yet when it moves from inside, it does not move naturally, the way fire does. For as long as fire exists, it never ceases its motion; but a body, once it has died, stops moving, although it is still a body. Therefore, since it is moved neither from outside like inanimate things, nor naturally like fire, it is evident that it is moved by the soul, which also supplies it with life. Thus, if it is established that life is supplied to our body by the soul, the soul is also known from its effects.
